architecture|internet software architect: The interaction/relation among components; in a web application, among UI, database and logic, with the focus on reliability, scalability, security, ease of implementation, modularity (slide 5). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
architectural pattern|architectural patt: A known way to structure a system that helps evaluate trade-offs (efficiency, maintenance cost, scalability, security, modularity) before committing to a design (slides 6–7). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
monolithic architecture|monolith|monolit: All application logic (UI, business logic, data access) bundled together in one deployable unit, usually on one machine and in one backend stack (slides 11, 19). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
deployable unit: The piece of software that is shut down, rebuilt and redeployed as a whole; a monolith has exactly one (slides 10–11). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
layered architecture|n-tier|n-tier archi: Code separated into layers, each handling one responsibility: presentation, business, application, data access (slides 12–13). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
presentation layer|UI layer: The layer where interaction with the end-user is handled, e.g. a form page (slide 13). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
business layer|business logic: The layer that controls the application's logic, e.g. decision making, routing requests (slide 13). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
application layer: The layer where the core functions of the app are implemented, e.g. libraries (slide 13). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
data access layer: The layer where access and retrieval of data are handled, e.g. databases (slide 13). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
microservices|microservice architecture|: A collection of loosely coupled, independently deployable services, each carrying one function and communicating via API (slides 14, 18, 20). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
SOA|service-oriented architecture: Service-Oriented Architecture; slightly different from MSA but refers to the same thing in this course (slide 18). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
loosely coupled: Almost independent; a loosely coupled service can be updated, moved to another machine or rewritten in another stack without the others (slides 18, 20). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
orchestration: Coordinating many services and their API calls; a cost of microservices together with monitoring and careful API design (slide 20). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
single point of failure: One component whose failure brings the whole design down, such as a database every request depends on (slide 8). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
reliability|reliable: Works correctly and consistently under normal conditions (slide 16). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
robustness|robust: Handles bad input or unexpected conditions safely, e.g. invalid JSON returns 400 Bad Request and the API does not crash (slide 16). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
resilience|resilient: Continues essential service or recovers after disruption, e.g. the store still sells when recommendations fail (slide 16). See [Monolithic, layered and microservice architectures](#/comp4537-l2/architecture-and-its-patterns).
API-centric|API centric: Built so every part is reached through an API, which lets a service in another stack be hooked up later (slides 7, 21). See [The course's API-centric microservice architecture](#/comp4537-l2/api-centric-microservices).
API gateway|gateway: The single component in touch with the outside world; client scripts send their AJAX API calls to it and it talks to the services and returns JSON (slides 8, 22). See [The course's API-centric microservice architecture](#/comp4537-l2/api-centric-microservices).
different origin: Client and servers are not hosted on the same machine; HTML files and Node.js files are on different machines (slide 21). See [The course's API-centric microservice architecture](#/comp4537-l2/api-centric-microservices).
CRUD: Create, Read, Update and Delete operations on a database via API requests (slide 24). See [The course's API-centric microservice architecture](#/comp4537-l2/api-centric-microservices).
versioning|API versioning: Putting the API version in the URL so old clients keep working, e.g. mydomain.com/V1/API/Patients/1 and /V1.1/ (slide 24). See [The course's API-centric microservice architecture](#/comp4537-l2/api-centric-microservices).
swagger: The tool the course uses to document and write specifications of an API (slide 23). See [The course's API-centric microservice architecture](#/comp4537-l2/api-centric-microservices).
JSON|JavaScript Object Notation: The standard string format for sending data between machines; responses from services are often JSON (slides 26–27). See [JSON.stringify serializes, JSON.parse deserializes](#/comp4537-l2/json-stringify-and-parse).
serialize|serialization|serialise: Flatten an in-memory object into a string any machine can read; JSON.stringify does it (slides 27–28). See [JSON.stringify serializes, JSON.parse deserializes](#/comp4537-l2/json-stringify-and-parse).
deserialize|deserialization|deserialise: Turn a JSON string back into an object; JSON.parse does it (slide 28). See [JSON.stringify serializes, JSON.parse deserializes](#/comp4537-l2/json-stringify-and-parse).
JSON.stringify|stringify: Object → JSON string (serialize); its result's typeof is "string" (slide 28). See [JSON.stringify serializes, JSON.parse deserializes](#/comp4537-l2/json-stringify-and-parse).
JSON.parse|parse: JSON string → object (deserialize); then navigate with dot notation and array indices (slides 28–29). See [JSON.stringify serializes, JSON.parse deserializes](#/comp4537-l2/json-stringify-and-parse).
web storage|HTML web storage|Web Storage: Client-side storage inside the browser, per origin, generally 5MB or more; localStorage and sessionStorage (slides 30, 32). See [localStorage and sessionStorage, per origin, strings only](#/comp4537-l2/web-storage).
localStorage|window.localStorage: The web storage object that stores data with no expiration date (slide 33). See [localStorage and sessionStorage, per origin, strings only](#/comp4537-l2/web-storage).
sessionStorage|window.sessionStorage: The web storage object that stores data for one session; data is lost when the browser tab is closed (slide 33). See [localStorage and sessionStorage, per origin, strings only](#/comp4537-l2/web-storage).
origin|same origin: Protocol and domain (the slide's words; the full rule adds the port); all pages from the same origin share the same storage in the same browser (slide 32). See [localStorage and sessionStorage, per origin, strings only](#/comp4537-l2/web-storage).
setItem: LocalStorage.setItem(key, value) stores a name/value pair; the value is stored as a string (slide 34). See [localStorage and sessionStorage, per origin, strings only](#/comp4537-l2/web-storage).
getItem: LocalStorage.getItem(key) retrieves the stored string, or null when the key is not there (slides 34, 37). See [localStorage and sessionStorage, per origin, strings only](#/comp4537-l2/web-storage).
removeItem: LocalStorage.removeItem(key) removes a single item (slide 34). See [localStorage and sessionStorage, per origin, strings only](#/comp4537-l2/web-storage).
clear|localStorage.clear: Removes everything stored for this origin (slide 34). See [localStorage and sessionStorage, per origin, strings only](#/comp4537-l2/web-storage).
Application tab: The Chrome DevTools (F12) tab whose Storage → Local Storage section shows, edits and deletes the key-value pairs for the current origin (slide 38). See [localStorage and sessionStorage, per origin, strings only](#/comp4537-l2/web-storage).
XSS|cross-site scripting: Injected JavaScript running on the page; because any script can read localStorage, one XSS hole exposes what is stored there (slides 43–44). See [localStorage and sessionStorage, per origin, strings only](#/comp4537-l2/web-storage).
HttpOnly cookie|HttpOnly: A cookie JavaScript cannot access; with Secure, often safer than localStorage for an authentication token (slide 44). See [localStorage and sessionStorage, per origin, strings only](#/comp4537-l2/web-storage).
